# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

For factual questions that require knowledge about IBM products, platforms, languages, commands, APIs, configuration, documented behavior, compatibility, or product-specific errors, consult IBM documentation before answering.
This includes technologies such as IBM i, IBM Z, z/OS, Db2, CICS, COBOL, JCL, RPG, AIX, and watsonx, even when the user does not explicitly say IBM.
For Bob(or IBM Bob) product questions, call `search_ibm_docs` directly with `library_name: "bob"`.
For other IBM products, first call `list_ibm_doc_libraries`, select the most relevant exact library name from its response, and then call `search_ibm_docs`. Do not invent or modify library names.
You may reuse a library name already returned in the current conversation for follow-up questions about the same product.
Base factual product claims on the retrieved documentation. If no suitable library or relevant documentation is found, say so rather than guessing.
Documentation lookup is unnecessary when the request is purely about code in the workspace and does not require IBM product knowledge.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

Call the tool with:

The `wrapText` function uses a template literal to split on `[-_\s]+`. The regex `[-_\s]+` - the issue referenced in the fix plan is "`service` renders as `ervice`". This happens when the regex is put inside a template string incorrectly. Let me check the actual template string context:

The `wrapText` function splits on `/[-_\s]+/`. But this is in a TypeScript template literal. The `\s` inside a template literal in a TypeScript source file would be fine since it would be output as `\s` in the raw string. Let me check the compiled output:

Good - the compiled output shows `text.split(/[-_\s]+/)` which is correct. The bug described in Phase 5.2 about `service` rendering as `ervice` might be in a different area. Let me look closer at the split — the regex `/[-_\s]+/` would split `service` correctly. But wait — looking at line 386 of the source: `const words = text.split(/[-_\s]+/);` — that works fine. But this is a template literal in TypeScript, so `\s` might be interpolated. Let me check the raw source more carefully:
This is inside the template literal (part of the HTML string returned). The function starts at line 384 but the surrounding template literal uses backticks. Let me look at the boundaries:

Found 1 matches
packages/vscode-extension/src/webview/graphHtml.ts:
  Line 18:   return `<!DOCTYPE html>

So the entire HTML is one big template literal starting at line 18. The `wrapText` function appears within that template literal at line 384. Let me check what's around the `\s` in the compiled output more carefully vs the source:

Error from tool execute_command: Exit code: 1

Command failed with exit code 1: /bin/zsh -c 'grep -n '\''split.*\\\\s\|split.*\\.s\|split.*\\/\[-'\'' packages/vscode-extension/src/webview/graphHtml.ts'

Error from tool execute_command: Exit code: 1

Stderr:
cat: illegal option -- A
usage: cat [-belnstuv] [file ...]

The source has `\s` properly escaped in the template literal. The compiled dist shows the same. So the `wrapText` splitting looks fine. Let me check if the bug is somewhere else — maybe in a label property name that uses `s`:

Actually, the fix plan says "Fix template-string escaping of the whitespace regex so `service` does not render as `ervice`". This might mean a different regex — one that strips leading `s` from `service`. Let me look for the issue more carefully in the graphHtml.ts:

The `wrapText` with `/[-_\s]+/` is not producing a bug here as the regex is correct. The "service → ervice" bug from the fix plan must be about the `\s` escaping in the template literal. Since the entire JavaScript code is embedded in a TypeScript template literal, if you write `\s` inside the template, it actually becomes `s` in the output because `\s` is a template escape where `\s` is not a valid escape sequence and TypeScript processes it as just `s`. Let me verify:
const x = text.split(/[-_s]+/);

There it is! In a JavaScript/TypeScript template literal, `\s` is not a valid escape and becomes just `s`. So in the source, `text.split(/[-_\s]+/)` inside the template literal compiles to `text.split(/[-_s]+/)` in the output — and `s` is a literal character, so "service" would split at `s` → `"ervice"` and `"ervice"` are the words. The fix is to double-escape: `\\s`:
const x = text.split(/[-_\s]+/);

Confirmed. Let me now fix this and the other critical issues. I'll address multiple fixes in parallel:

**Fix 3: MCP `handleAnalyzeChange` uses wrong repo path and wrong baseline**
**Fix 4: incrementalAnalysis/dirtyIncrementalAnalysis dispatch for node/python/go**

data.content: Now fix the MCP `handleAnalyzeChange` — it uses `svc.identity.rootPath` as the Git repo but should use `svc.identity.repository`. Also the critical bug: after `getOrAnalyze()` caches the result, `getLastAnalyzedCommit` returns the current HEAD, making `lastCommit === currentCommit` always true → "No changes":

async function handleAnalyzeChange(serviceArg: string) {
  const result = await getOrAnalyze();
  const svc = resolveService(serviceArg, result.services);

  // Detect current HEAD and compare with cached
  const git = new GitAnalyzer(svc.identity.rootPath);
  const currentCommit = git.getHead(false);
  const lastCommit = engine.getCache().getLastAnalyzedCommit(svc.identity.serviceId);

  if (!lastCommit) {
    return {
      content: [
        {
          type: 'text',
          text: JSON.stringify({
            serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
            message: 'No previous analysis found. Run refresh_context to generate initial context.',
          }),
        },
      ],
    };
  }

  if (lastCommit === currentCommit) {
    return {
      content: [
        {
          type: 'text',
          text: JSON.stringify({
            serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
            message: 'No changes detected since last analysis.',
            commit: currentCommit.slice(0, 7),
            status: 'No changes',
          }),
        },
      ],
    };
  }

  // Get changed files
  const changedFiles = git.getChangedFiles(lastCommit, currentCommit);
  const changeSet: ChangeSet = {
    serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
    oldCommit: lastCommit,
    newCommit: currentCommit,
    changedFiles,
    affectsApi: changedFiles.some(f => f.category === 'API'),
    affectsDatabase: changedFiles.some(f => f.category === 'ENTITY'),
    affectsDependencies: changedFiles.some(f => ['SERVICE', 'CONFIG'].includes(f.category)),
  };

  // Run impact analysis
  const relatedServices = result.services.filter(s => s.identity.serviceId !== svc.identity.serviceId);
  let impactReport;

  if (watsonxRuntime) {
    impactReport = await watsonxRuntime.analyzeImpact(changeSet, svc, relatedServices);
  } else {
    const { WatsonxRuntime: WR } = await import('@bob-context-graph/watsonx');
    const { WatsonxClient: WC } = await import('@bob-context-graph/watsonx');
    const mockClient = new WC({ apiKey: '', projectId: '' });
    const runtime = new WR(mockClient);
    impactReport = await runtime.analyzeImpact(changeSet, svc, relatedServices);
  }

  const response = {
    serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
    change: {
      oldCommit: lastCommit.slice(0, 7),
      newCommit: currentCommit.slice(0, 7),
      changedFileCount: changedFiles.length,
      affectedAreas: {
        api: changeSet.affectsApi,
        database: changeSet.affectsDatabase,
        dependencies: changeSet.affectsDependencies,
      },
      changedFiles: changedFiles.slice(0, 20).map(f => ({
        path: f.path,
        category: f.category,
        changeType: f.changeType,
      })),
    },
    impactReport,
  };

  return {
    content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify(response, null, 2) }],
  };
}

async function handleAnalyzeChange(serviceArg: string) {
  // F03: get context WITHOUT advancing the comparison baseline.
  // getOrAnalyze() already has an up-to-date in-memory snapshot; calling it here
  // does NOT re-index, so the baselineCommit stored in the cache is unchanged.
  const result = await getOrAnalyze();
  const svc = resolveService(serviceArg, result.services);

  // Use the repository root (not the service rootPath) for Git operations
  const git = new GitAnalyzer(svc.identity.repository);
  const currentCommit = git.getHead(false);
  const currentDirty = git.getDirtyHash();

  // F03: compare against the stored baseline commit, not lastAnalyzedCommit.
  // baselineCommit is the commit that was indexed BEFORE the most recent analysis,
  // so it correctly represents the "before" side of any pending change.
  const baselineCommit = engine.getCache().getBaselineCommit(svc.identity.serviceId);
  const lastAnalyzedCommit = engine.getCache().getLastAnalyzedCommit(svc.identity.serviceId);

  if (!lastAnalyzedCommit) {
    return {
      content: [
        {
          type: 'text',
          text: JSON.stringify({
            serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
            message: 'No previous analysis found. Run refresh_context to generate initial context.',
          }),
        },
      ],
    };
  }

  // Determine the effective comparison baseline:
  // Use baselineCommit (the pre-index snapshot) when available; otherwise fall back
  // to lastAnalyzedCommit so we at least detect a committed vs. dirty difference.
  const effectiveBaseline = baselineCommit ?? lastAnalyzedCommit;

  // No committed change and no dirty state → truly no changes
  if (effectiveBaseline === currentCommit && currentDirty === 'clean') {
    return {
      content: [
        {
          type: 'text',
          text: JSON.stringify({
            serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
            message: 'No changes detected since last analysis.',
            commit: currentCommit.slice(0, 7),
            status: 'No changes',
          }),
        },
      ],
    };
  }

  // Build the combined changeset: committed diff + dirty files
  const committedChanges = effectiveBaseline !== currentCommit
    ? git.getChangedFiles(effectiveBaseline, currentCommit)
    : [];
  const dirtyFiles = currentDirty !== 'clean' ? git.getDirtyFiles() : [];

  // Scope to this service's subdirectory within the repo
  const { GitAnalyzer: GA } = await import('@bob-context-graph/core');
  const serviceRelPath = require('path').relative(svc.identity.repository, svc.identity.rootPath).replace(/\\/g, '/');
  const prefix = serviceRelPath ? serviceRelPath + '/' : '';
  const filteredCommitted = prefix ? committedChanges.filter((f: { path: string }) => f.path.startsWith(prefix)) : committedChanges;
  const filteredDirty = prefix ? dirtyFiles.filter((f: { path: string }) => f.path.startsWith(prefix)) : dirtyFiles;

  // Merge (dirty wins over committed for the same path)
  const mergedMap = new Map<string, typeof filteredCommitted[0]>();
  for (const f of filteredCommitted) mergedMap.set(f.path, f);
  for (const f of filteredDirty) mergedMap.set(f.path, f);
  const changedFiles = Array.from(mergedMap.values());

  if (changedFiles.length === 0) {
    return {
      content: [
        {
          type: 'text',
          text: JSON.stringify({
            serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
            message: 'No changes detected in this service since last analysis.',
            commit: currentCommit.slice(0, 7),
            status: 'No changes',
          }),
        },
      ],
    };
  }

  const changeSet: ChangeSet = {
    serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
    oldCommit: effectiveBaseline,
    newCommit: currentCommit,
    changedFiles,
    affectsApi: changedFiles.some(f => f.category === 'API'),
    affectsDatabase: changedFiles.some(f => f.category === 'ENTITY'),
    affectsDependencies: changedFiles.some(f => ['SERVICE', 'CONFIG'].includes(f.category)),
  };

  // Run impact analysis
  const relatedServices = result.services.filter(s => s.identity.serviceId !== svc.identity.serviceId);
  let impactReport;

  if (watsonxRuntime) {
    impactReport = await watsonxRuntime.analyzeImpact(changeSet, svc, relatedServices);
  } else {
    const { WatsonxRuntime: WR } = await import('@bob-context-graph/watsonx');
    const { WatsonxClient: WC } = await import('@bob-context-graph/watsonx');
    const mockClient = new WC({ apiKey: '', projectId: '' });
    const runtime = new WR(mockClient);
    impactReport = await runtime.analyzeImpact(changeSet, svc, relatedServices);
  }

  const response = {
    serviceId: svc.identity.serviceId,
    change: {
      oldCommit: effectiveBaseline.slice(0, 7),
      newCommit: currentCommit.slice(0, 7),
      dirtyState: currentDirty !== 'clean' ? 'dirty' : 'clean',
      changedFileCount: changedFiles.length,
      affectedAreas: {
        api: changeSet.affectsApi,
        database: changeSet.affectsDatabase,
        dependencies: changeSet.affectsDependencies,
      },
      changedFiles: changedFiles.slice(0, 20).map(f => ({
        path: f.path,
        category: f.category,
        changeType: f.changeType,
      })),
    },
    impactReport,
  };

  return {
    content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify(response, null, 2) }],
  };
}

  getDirtyFiles(): ChangedFile[] {
    try {
      // Use NUL-delimited output (-z) to handle paths with spaces and special characters.
      // Each record is: XY<SP>path<NUL>  (or XY<SP>old<NUL>new<NUL> for renames)
      const output = execSync('git status --porcelain=v1 -z', {
        cwd: this.repoPath,
        encoding: 'utf8',
        stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
      });

      if (!output) return [];

      const results: ChangedFile[] = [];
      // Split on NUL; each non-empty token is one entry
      const tokens = output.split('\0').filter(t => t.length > 0);

      for (let i = 0; i < tokens.length; i++) {
        const token = tokens[i];
        // XY status is always the first 2 chars; path follows after a space
        const xy = token.slice(0, 2);
        // For renames (R/C), the porcelain -z format outputs:
        //   "XY new_path\0old_path" — the next token is the old path
        const isRename = xy[0] === 'R' || xy[0] === 'C' || xy[1] === 'R' || xy[1] === 'C';
        const filePath = token.slice(3); // skip XY + space
        if (isRename) {
          // skip the old-path token that follows
          i++;
        }
        const changeType = (xy.includes('D') ? 'deleted' :
          (xy.includes('A') || xy.trim() === '??') ? 'added' : 'modified') as ChangedFile['changeType'];
        results.push({ path: filePath.trim(), category: this.classifyFile(filePath.trim()), changeType });

The `generateServiceId` flattens paths replacing `/` with `-`, so `team-a/order-service` → `team-a-order-service` and `team/a-order-service` → `team-a-order-service` — same ID.   /**
   * F09: Generate a canonical, unique service ID.
   * Uses workspace-relative path so two services with the same dir name get different IDs.
   */
  generateServiceId(dirPath: string, repository?: string): string {
    // Make it relative to workspace root to avoid collision
    const relToWorkspace = path.relative(this.workspaceRoot, dirPath);
    // Normalize path separators and sanitize
    const normalized = relToWorkspace
      .replace(/\\/g, '/')
      .toLowerCase()
      .replace(/[^a-z0-9/-]/g, '-')
      .replace(/\/+/g, '-')

Now fix **POLY-node/python/go** — the incremental analysis for these stacks. Looking at the failure: `before` and `after` are identical. The issue is that after a committed file change, `incrementalAnalysis` checks `changeSet.affectsApi` — but the file is `api.js`/`api.py`/`handler.go`. Let me check what `classifyFile` returns for these:

- `api.js`: `basename.endsWith('.js')` → `SERVICE` (not `API`)
- `api.py`: `basename.endsWith('.py')` → `SERVICE` (not `API`)
- `handler.go`: `basename.endsWith('_handler.go')` → `API` ✓

So the fix needed for `classifyFile`: recognize common entry files as potentially containing routes. The plan says "Recognize common entry files as potentially containing routes instead of relying solely on controller-like filenames." The fix: for Node/Python/Go, if the file contains route definitions, it should be classified as `API`. But that requires reading content in `classifyFile`, which is a path-only function.

A simpler and correct fix: for non-spring stacks, when the changed file belongs to the service and is a `.js`/`.py`/`.go` file (even classified as `SERVICE`), re-run the API parser to check if routes changed. This is phase 4.1 — "Recognize common entry files as potentially containing routes":

The condition is `changeSet.affectsApi` but for `api.js`/`api.py`/`routes.js`, `classifyFile` returns `SERVICE` not `API`. The fix: for non-spring stacks, also re-parse when SERVICE files change (since any .js/.py/.go file could contain routes):

Now fix **BRANCH** — when you checkout the same HEAD but different branch, the cached discovery metadata has the old branch. The fix: read branch independently from git each time, not from cached discovery:

The branch is read in `WorkspaceScanner.analyzeDirectory()` via `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`. This happens during discovery. But if the workspace fingerprint cache skips discovery, the cached `DiscoveredService.branch` from `reconstructDiscoveredFromCache` has stale branch. Let me check:
The `repoHeadMap` overrides `commitHash` but doesn't override `branch`. The branch comes from the cached `DiscoveredService`. Let me add branch overriding from a per-repo branch map:

Now fix **F02** — the incremental analysis marks all 3 services as `refreshed` (0 cached) when only 1 service commit changes. The issue: `incrementalAnalysis` returns `status = 'Changed'`. When the engine calls `analyzeService` with `lastAnalyzedCommit !== commitHash`, it runs `incrementalAnalysis` for ALL services. But for unchanged services, the commit IS the same (they share the monorepo's HEAD). So the problem is something else.

Looking at the test: `F02 Commit refreshes 1 / caches 2` with `actual: {cached:0, refreshed:3}`. After a commit to one service, ALL 3 are refreshed. The likely issue: the `lastAnalyzedCommit` in cache stores the OLD HEAD for all services. After the commit, the current HEAD advances. Now all 3 services have `lastAnalyzedCommit = oldHEAD !== newHEAD` → all 3 run `incrementalAnalysis`.

The fix: during incremental analysis, check if the changed files scope to this service. If the changeset for a service is empty, return the cached context as `Cached` instead of `Changed`:

# BOB CONTEXT GRAPH
## Incremental System Intelligence for IBM Bob

**Tagline:**  
Bob shouldn't rediscover your system every time you ask a question.

## 1. PROJECT GOAL

Build **Bob Context Graph**, an extension of IBM Bob that provides persistent, commit-aware understanding of a microservice architecture.

The system should allow Bob to understand:

- Microservices in the current workspace
- REST APIs exposed by each service
- API contracts and relevant models
- Database entities, tables, columns, and relationships
- Dependencies between services
- Dependencies between services and databases
- Changes between Git commits
- The potential blast radius of API or database schema changes

The key optimization is that Bob should NOT repeatedly read and rediscover repositories that have not changed.

Each analyzed service should have a structured semantic context cached against its latest Git commit hash.

When the repository has not changed, Bob should reuse the cached context.

When the repository changes, the system should use Git diff to identify the changed files and update only the affected context.

IBM watsonx should be used for semantic understanding and change-impact reasoning rather than basic deterministic repository discovery.

The final system should integrate with IBM Bob through MCP and a Bob Skill while providing a visual interface through a VS Code extension distributed as a downloadable `.vsix`.

---

# 2. CORE PRODUCT CONCEPT

The architecture should conceptually work as follows:

Developer
→ IBM Bob
→ Bob Skill
→ MCP Client
→ Bob Context Graph MCP Server
→ Context Graph
→ Deterministic Repository Analyzer

# BOB CONTEXT GRAPH
## Incremental System Intelligence for IBM Bob

**Tagline:**  
Bob shouldn't rediscover your system every time you ask a question.

## 1. PROJECT GOAL

Build **Bob Context Graph**, an extension of IBM Bob that provides persistent, commit-aware understanding of a microservice architecture.

The system should allow Bob to understand:

- Microservices in the current workspace
- REST APIs exposed by each service
- API contracts and relevant models
- Database entities, tables, columns, and relationships
- Dependencies between services
- Dependencies between services and databases
- Changes between Git commits
- The potential blast radius of API or database schema changes

The key optimization is that Bob should NOT repeatedly read and rediscover repositories that have not changed.

Each analyzed service should have a structured semantic context cached against its latest Git commit hash.

When the repository has not changed, Bob should reuse the cached context.

When the repository changes, the system should use Git diff to identify the changed files and update only the affected context.

IBM watsonx should be used for semantic understanding and change-impact reasoning rather than basic deterministic repository discovery.

The final system should integrate with IBM Bob through MCP and a Bob Skill while providing a visual interface through a VS Code extension distributed as a downloadable `.vsix`.

---

# 2. CORE PRODUCT CONCEPT

The architecture should conceptually work as follows:

Developer
→ IBM Bob
→ Bob Skill
→ MCP Client
→ Bob Context Graph MCP Server
→ Context Graph
→ Deterministic Repository Analyzer
→ IBM watsonx Runtime

The VS Code extension should visualize the same Context Graph.

Responsibilities:

**VSIX**
See the system.

**MCP**
Allow Bob to access the system intelligence.

**Bob Skill**
Teach Bob when and how to use the capability.

**watsonx**
Reason about semantic meaning and change impact.

**IBM Bob**
Plan and act on the resulting system intelligence.

Do NOT attempt to replace Bob's existing coding capabilities.

---

# 3. TARGET TECHNOLOGY SCOPE

For the hackathon prototype, optimize for ONE supported backend stack.

Preferred demo stack:

- Java
- Spring Boot
- PostgreSQL
- Git
- REST APIs

Minimum Spring concepts to recognize:

- `@RestController`
- `@RequestMapping`
- `@GetMapping`

- `@DeleteMapping`
- `@Entity`
- `@Table`
- `@Column`
- `@Id`
- `@ManyToOne`
- `@OneToMany`
- DTO/model references

Do NOT attempt universal programming-language support during the 14-hour build.

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.

The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

For factual questions that require knowledge about IBM products, platforms, languages, commands, APIs, configuration, documented behavior, compatibility, or product-specific errors, consult IBM documentation before answering.
This includes technologies such as IBM i, IBM Z, z/OS, Db2, CICS, COBOL, JCL, RPG, AIX, and watsonx, even when the user does not explicitly say IBM.
For Bob(or IBM Bob) product questions, call `search_ibm_docs` directly with `library_name: "bob"`.
For other IBM products, first call `list_ibm_doc_libraries`, select the most relevant exact library name from its response, and then call `search_ibm_docs`. Do not invent or modify library names.
You may reuse a library name already returned in the current conversation for follow-up questions about the same product.
Base factual product claims on the retrieved documentation. If no suitable library or relevant documentation is found, say so rather than guessing.
Documentation lookup is unnecessary when the request is purely about code in the workspace and does not require IBM product knowledge.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

You have access to workflows that provide specialized multi-step processes for specific tasks. Review the available workflows below. When a user's request matches a workflow's purpose, use the start_workflow tool. Run the workflow only if you are sure the workflow description will provide appropriate assistance. When suggesting workflows to users, provide the title and description, never the internal ID.
Available workflows:
* create_pr_workflow: Create Pull Request - Generates description from git diff using PR templates, allows review and editing, then creates the pull request on GitHub.

# BOB CONTEXT GRAPH
## Incremental System Intelligence for IBM Bob

**Tagline:**  
Bob shouldn't rediscover your system every time you ask a question.

## 1. PROJECT GOAL

Build **Bob Context Graph**, an extension of IBM Bob that provides persistent, commit-aware understanding of a microservice architecture.

The system should allow Bob to understand:

- Microservices in the current workspace
- REST APIs exposed by each service
- API contracts and relevant models
- Database entities, tables, columns, and relationships
- Dependencies between services
- Dependencies between services and databases
- Changes between Git commits
- The potential blast radius of API or database schema changes

The key optimization is that Bob should NOT repeatedly read and rediscover repositories that have not changed.

Each analyzed service should have a structured semantic context cached against its latest Git commit hash.

When the repository has not changed, Bob should reuse the cached context.

When the repository changes, the system should use Git diff to identify the changed files and update only the affected context.

IBM watsonx should be used for semantic understanding and change-impact reasoning rather than basic deterministic repository discovery.

The final system should integrate with IBM Bob through MCP and a Bob Skill while providing a visual interface through a VS Code extension distributed as a downloadable `.vsix`.

---

# 2. CORE PRODUCT CONCEPT

The architecture should conceptually work as follows:

Developer
→ IBM Bob
→ Bob Skill
→ MCP Client
→ Bob Context Graph MCP Server
→ Context Graph
→ Deterministic Repository Analyzer
→ IBM watsonx Runtime

The VS Code extension should visualize the same Context Graph.

Responsibilities:

**VSIX**
See the system.

**MCP**
Allow Bob to access the system intelligence.

**Bob Skill**
Teach Bob when and how to use the capability.

**watsonx**
Reason about semantic meaning and change impact.

**IBM Bob**
Plan and act on the resulting system intelligence.

Do NOT attempt to replace Bob's existing coding capabilities.

---

# 3. TARGET TECHNOLOGY SCOPE

For the hackathon prototype, optimize for ONE supported backend stack.

Preferred demo stack:

- Java
- Spring Boot
- PostgreSQL
- Git
- REST APIs

Minimum Spring concepts to recognize:

- `@RestController`
- `@RequestMapping`
- `@GetMapping`
- `@PostMapping`
- `@PutMapping`
- `@DeleteMapping`
- `@Entity`
- `@Table`
- `@Column`
- `@Id`
- `@ManyToOne`
- `@OneToMany`
- DTO/model references

Do NOT attempt universal programming-language support during the 14-hour build.

---

# 4. HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE

IBM Bob
    |
    | Bob Skill
    |
    | MCP
    v
Bob Context Graph MCP Server
    |
    +-- Git Analyzer
    |
    +-- API Analyzer
    |
    +-- Database Schema Analyzer
    |
    +-- Dependency Analyzer
    |
    +-- Context Cache
    |
    +-- Context Graph
    |
    +-- watsonx Runtime
            |
            +-- Semantic Summary
            +-- Change Interpretation
            +-- Impact Reasoning
            +-- Migration Recommendations

VS Code VSIX
    |
    +-- System Overview
    +-- Service Explorer
    +-- Dependency Graph
    +-- Change Detection
    +-- Impact Analysis

---

# 5. P0 — WORKSPACE DISCOVERY

Implement automatic workspace discovery.

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect workspace root
- [ ] Discover microservice directories
- [ ] Detect Git repositories
- [ ] Determine repository name
- [ ] Determine current Git branch
- [ ] Determine latest commit hash
- [ ] Generate unique service ID
- [ ] Display discovered services in VSIX
- [ ] Display service analysis status

Supported statuses:

- Indexed
- Cached
- Changed
- Analyzing
- Error

Example:

SYSTEM OVERVIEW

3 Services

✓ order-service
  commit a91fc20
  Cached

✓ inventory-service
  commit 12ab19f
  Cached

⚠ payment-service
  commit 9ff182a
  Changed

---

# 6. P0 — COMMIT-AWARE SEMANTIC CACHE

This is one of the primary features.

Every analyzed service must have a structured context associated with its Git state.

Recommended cache identity:

repository + branch + commitHash

Example:

{
  "service": "order-service",
  "branch": "main",
  "commit": "a91fc20",
  "summary": "...",
  "apis": [],
  "database": [],
  "dependencies": [],
  "events": []
}

Required behavior:

- [ ] Read repository HEAD
- [ ] Compare HEAD with cached commit
- [ ] Cache hit → reuse existing context
- [ ] Cache miss → analyze repository
- [ ] Store generated context
- [ ] Display cache status in VSIX
- [ ] Store previous analyzed commit for incremental comparison

Example UI:

ORDER SERVICE

Commit:
a91fc20

Context:
✓ Cached

Files:
42

Last Analysis:
10:41:22

Estimated Context Reuse:
~31K tokens avoided

Any token-saving metric must be clearly presented as an estimate.

---

# 7. P0 — INCREMENTAL ANALYSIS

Do not automatically rescan an entire repository whenever HEAD changes.

Compare:

OLD COMMIT
a91fc20

NEW COMMIT
c821ad3

Use Git diff to identify changes.

Conceptually:

git diff --name-only a91fc20 c821ad3

Pipeline:

Commit changed
→ Git diff
→ Changed files
→ Classify files
→ Determine affected artifacts
→ Re-analyze affected context
→ Update Context Graph
→ Update cache

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect commit change
- [ ] Calculate Git diff
- [ ] Identify changed files
- [ ] Classify changed files
- [ ] Determine whether API is affected
- [ ] Determine whether database schema is affected
- [ ] Determine whether service dependency is affected
- [ ] Re-analyze changed service only
- [ ] Preserve unaffected service contexts
- [ ] Update cache
- [ ] Update Context Graph

---

# 8. P0 — API INTELLIGENCE

Extract REST APIs from each supported Spring Boot service.

Example:

Order Service

GET    /orders/{id}
POST   /orders
PUT    /orders/{id}
DELETE /orders/{id}

For each endpoint, attempt to capture:

- HTTP method
- Endpoint path
- Controller
- Request model
- Response model
- Related service dependencies
- Related database entities
- Semantic description

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect REST controllers
- [ ] Detect HTTP methods
- [ ] Detect endpoint paths
- [ ] Detect request models where possible
- [ ] Detect response models where possible
- [ ] Associate API with service
- [ ] Associate API with relevant entity where possible
- [ ] Generate short semantic description using watsonx

Example semantic description:

"Creates an order, validates inventory availability, persists the order, and initiates payment."

---

# 9. P0 — DATABASE SCHEMA INTELLIGENCE

Extract basic database structure from Spring/JPA entities.

Example:

orders

├── id : UUID
├── customer_id : INTEGER
├── product_id : UUID
├── quantity : INTEGER
└── status : VARCHAR

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect JPA entities
- [ ] Detect table names
- [ ] Detect columns
- [ ] Detect basic data types
- [ ] Detect primary keys where possible
- [ ] Detect entity relationships
- [ ] Associate tables with services
- [ ] Store database schema in ServiceContext
- [ ] Add database nodes to Context Graph

Advanced Flyway/Liquibase support is P1, not required for P0.

---

# 10. P0 — SERVICE CONTEXT MODEL

Each service should produce a normalized ServiceContext.

Conceptual structure:

ServiceContext

├── identity
│   ├── serviceId
│   ├── repository
│   ├── branch
│   └── commitHash
│
├── APIs
│   ├── endpoints
│   ├── requestSchemas
│   └── responseSchemas
│
├── Database
│   ├── tables
│   ├── columns
│   └── relationships
│
├── Dependencies
│   ├── upstream
│   └── downstream
│
├── Events
│   ├── publishes
│   └── consumes
│
└── semanticSummary

Events can remain minimal or empty for the P0 demo if necessary.

---

# 11. P0 — SYSTEM CONTEXT GRAPH

Combine all ServiceContexts into a System Context Graph.

Example:

                  ORDER
                 SERVICE
                 /     \
                /       \
               v         v
        INVENTORY      PAYMENT
         SERVICE       SERVICE
            |             |
            v             v
       inventory_db   payment_db

              |
              v
           orders_db

Required node types:

- Service
- Database

Optional P1 node types:

- API
- Event
- Table

Required edges:

- Service → Service dependency
- Service → Database ownership/use

Checklist:

- [ ] Build graph from ServiceContexts
- [ ] Create service nodes
- [ ] Create database nodes
- [ ] Create dependency edges
- [ ] Create database edges
- [ ] Render graph in VSIX
- [ ] Support zoom
- [ ] Support pan
- [ ] Make nodes clickable
- [ ] Display selected node information
- [ ] Visually distinguish services and databases

The graph can be read-only.

Do NOT build a graph editor.

---

# 12. P0 — CHANGE IMPACT ANALYSIS

This is the primary AI feature.

Example change:

orders.customer_id

INTEGER
→
UUID

Pipeline:

Git Diff
→ Change Detector
→ Context Graph
→ Retrieve Related Nodes
→ Structured Change Context
→ watsonx Runtime
→ Impact Reasoning
→ Bob + VSIX

Expected output:

CHANGE IMPACT

Change:
orders.customer_id
INTEGER → UUID

HIGH
payment-service

Reason:
OrderCreatedEvent currently expects an INTEGER customerId.

MEDIUM
Order REST API

Reason:
The customer identifier is exposed through the API contract.

LOW
Frontend

Reason:
The frontend already represents customer identifiers as strings.

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect API changes
- [ ] Detect database schema changes
- [ ] Identify affected graph nodes
- [ ] Retrieve related service contexts
- [ ] Construct scoped watsonx prompt/context
- [ ] Generate impact explanation
- [ ] Generate severity
- [ ] Explain WHY a component is affected
- [ ] Suggest affected components/files where possible
- [ ] Generate migration recommendations

Severity levels:

HIGH
MEDIUM
LOW

Severity must include an explanation rather than only a label.

---

# 13. P0 — IBM WATSONX RUNTIME

watsonx must NOT be responsible for basic deterministic repository discovery when conventional tooling can do it more reliably.

Do NOT use:

Entire Repository
→ LLM
→ "Figure everything out"

Prefer:

Git + Parser + Structured Extraction
→ Structured Facts
→ Context Graph
→ Scoped Context
→ watsonx
→ Semantic Reasoning

watsonx responsibilities:

- [ ] Service semantic summaries
- [ ] API semantic descriptions
- [ ] Change interpretation
- [ ] Impact reasoning
- [ ] Severity reasoning
- [ ] Human-readable explanations
- [ ] Migration/change recommendations

The project should demonstrate that watsonx receives relevant scoped context instead of unnecessarily receiving the entire repository.

---

# 14. P0 — MCP SERVER

MCP is the primary integration contract between Bob and Bob Context Graph.

Minimum required MCP tools:

## get_system_context()

Returns:

- Services
- Current commit hashes
- Service relationships
- Database relationships
- System summary

Checklist:

- [ ] Implement tool
- [ ] Return structured response
- [ ] Verify Bob can call it

## get_service_context(service)

Returns:

- Service identity
- Commit
- APIs
- Database schema
- Dependencies
- Semantic summary

Checklist:

- [ ] Implement tool
- [ ] Validate service argument
- [ ] Return cached context where possible

## analyze_change(service)

Performs:

- Git diff
- Change classification
- Dependency lookup
- watsonx impact reasoning

Returns:

- Detected changes
- Affected components
- Severity
- Reasoning
- Recommended actions

Checklist:

- [ ] Implement tool
- [ ] Connect Git diff
- [ ] Connect Context Graph
- [ ] Connect watsonx
- [ ] Return structured impact report

## refresh_context(service?)

Allows Bob to explicitly refresh system intelligence.

Checklist:

- [ ] Refresh one service
- [ ] Optionally refresh all services
- [ ] Update cache
- [ ] Update graph

Optional MCP tools:

- [ ] get_dependency_graph()
- [ ] get_database_schema()
- [ ] get_api_contract()

Do not prioritize optional MCP tools until the four primary tools work.

---

# 15. P0 — IBM BOB MCP CONFIGURATION

The repository should include project-level Bob configuration.

Target:

.bob/
└── mcp.json

Configure Bob Context Graph MCP server so a developer cloning the repository can configure/run the integration with minimal manual work.

Checklist:

- [ ] Include `.bob/mcp.json`
- [ ] Document required environment variables
- [ ] Document watsonx credentials configuration
- [ ] Document MCP startup procedure
- [ ] Verify Bob discovers the MCP tools

Never commit credentials to Git.

---

# 16. P0 — BOB SKILL

Create:

.bob/
└── skills/
    └── context-graph/
        └── SKILL.md

The Skill should teach Bob that when a developer asks about:

- Architecture
- Microservice relationships
- API dependencies
- Database schema dependencies
- Breaking changes
- Change impact
- Blast radius
- Migration planning

Bob should query Bob Context Graph before independently rediscovering the entire repository.

Desired behavior:

"When architectural or change-impact context is required, first query Bob Context Graph MCP.

Prefer cached system context.

Use get_system_context() for architecture questions.

Use get_service_context(service) for service-specific questions.

Use analyze_change(service) when evaluating a Git/API/database change.

Inspect raw source code only when implementation-level details unavailable from the context graph are required."

Checklist:

- [ ] Create Skill
- [ ] Describe appropriate triggers
- [ ] Describe available MCP tools
- [ ] Tell Bob to prefer cached context
- [ ] Test at least one architecture question
- [ ] Test at least one impact-analysis question

---

# 17. P0 — VS CODE EXTENSION / VSIX

The VS Code extension is the visual interface for developers.

It is NOT the primary Bob integration layer.

Responsibilities:

- Display system state
- Display services
- Display cache state
- Display dependency graph
- Display detected changes

Minimum sidebar:

# 18. P0 — GRAPH WEBVIEW

Create a visual dependency graph inside VS Code.

Example:

│ Bob Context Graph              HEAD: c821ad3     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

Checklist:

---

# 19. P0 — IMPACT VISUALIZATION

When a breaking change is detected, visually highlight affected components.

## 1. PROJECT GOAL

Build **Bob Context Graph**, an extension of IBM Bob that provides persistent, commit-aware understanding of a microservice architecture.

IBM watsonx should be used for semantic understanding and change-impact reasoning rather than basic deterministic repository discovery.

# BOB CONTEXT GRAPH
## Incremental System Intelligence for IBM Bob

**Tagline:**  
Bob shouldn't rediscover your system every time you ask a question.

## 1. PROJECT GOAL

Build **Bob Context Graph**, an extension of IBM Bob that provides persistent, commit-aware understanding of a microservice architecture.

The system should allow Bob to understand:

- Microservices in the current workspace
- REST APIs exposed by each service
- API contracts and relevant models
- Database entities, tables, columns, and relationships
- Dependencies between services
- Dependencies between services and databases
- Changes between Git commits
- The potential blast radius of API or database schema changes

The key optimization is that Bob should NOT repeatedly read and rediscover repositories that have not changed.

Each analyzed service should have a structured semantic context cached against its latest Git commit hash.

When the repository has not changed, Bob should reuse the cached context.

When the repository changes, the system should use Git diff to identify the changed files and update only the affected context.

IBM watsonx should be used for semantic understanding and change-impact reasoning rather than basic deterministic repository discovery.

The final system should integrate with IBM Bob through MCP and a Bob Skill while providing a visual interface through a VS Code extension distributed as a downloadable `.vsix`.

arguments.content:
# BOB CONTEXT GRAPH
## Incremental System Intelligence for IBM Bob

**Tagline:**  
Bob shouldn't rediscover your system every time you ask a question.

## 1. PROJECT GOAL

Build **Bob Context Graph**, an extension of IBM Bob that provides persistent, commit-aware understanding of a microservice architecture.

The system should allow Bob to understand:

- Microservices in the current workspace
- REST APIs exposed by each service
- API contracts and relevant models
- Database entities, tables, columns, and relationships
- Dependencies between services
- Dependencies between services and databases
- Changes between Git commits
- The potential blast radius of API or database schema changes

The key optimization is that Bob should NOT repeatedly read and rediscover repositories that have not changed.

Each analyzed service should have a structured semantic context cached against its latest Git commit hash.

When the repository has not changed, Bob should reuse the cached context.

When the repository changes, the system should use Git diff to identify the changed files and update only the affected context.

IBM watsonx should be used for semantic understanding and change-impact reasoning rather than basic deterministic repository discovery.

The final system should integrate with IBM Bob through MCP and a Bob Skill while providing a visual interface through a VS Code extension distributed as a downloadable `.vsix`.

---

## 2. CORE PRODUCT CONCEPT

The architecture should conceptually work as follows:

```
Developer
→ IBM Bob
→ Bob Skill
→ MCP Client
→ Bob Context Graph MCP Server
→ Context Graph
→ Deterministic Repository Analyzer
→ IBM watsonx Runtime
```

The VS Code extension should visualize the same Context Graph.

Responsibilities:

**VSIX** — See the system.

**MCP** — Allow Bob to access the system intelligence.

**Bob Skill** — Teach Bob when and how to use the capability.

**watsonx** — Reason about semantic meaning and change impact.

**IBM Bob** — Plan and act on the resulting system intelligence.

Do NOT attempt to replace Bob's existing coding capabilities.

---

## 3. TARGET TECHNOLOGY SCOPE

For the hackathon prototype, optimize for ONE supported backend stack.

Preferred demo stack:

- Java
- Spring Boot
- PostgreSQL
- Git
- REST APIs

Minimum Spring concepts to recognize:

- `@RestController`
- `@RequestMapping`
- `@GetMapping`
- `@PostMapping`
- `@PutMapping`
- `@DeleteMapping`
- `@Entity`
- `@Table`
- `@Column`
- `@Id`
- `@ManyToOne`
- `@OneToMany`
- DTO/model references

Do NOT attempt universal programming-language support during the 14-hour build.

---

## 4. HIGH-LEVEL ARCHITECTURE

```
IBM Bob
    |
    | Bob Skill
    |
    | MCP
    v
Bob Context Graph MCP Server
    |
    +-- Git Analyzer
    |
    +-- API Analyzer
    |
    +-- Database Schema Analyzer
    |
    +-- Dependency Analyzer
    |
    +-- Context Cache
    |
    +-- Context Graph
    |
    +-- watsonx Runtime
            |
            +-- Semantic Summary
            +-- Change Interpretation
            +-- Impact Reasoning
            +-- Migration Recommendations

VS Code VSIX
    |
    +-- System Overview
    +-- Service Explorer
    +-- Dependency Graph
    +-- Change Detection
    +-- Impact Analysis
```

---

## 5. P0 — WORKSPACE DISCOVERY

Implement automatic workspace discovery.

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect workspace root
- [ ] Discover microservice directories
- [ ] Detect Git repositories
- [ ] Determine repository name
- [ ] Determine current Git branch
- [ ] Determine latest commit hash
- [ ] Generate unique service ID
- [ ] Display discovered services in VSIX
- [ ] Display service analysis status

Supported statuses:

- Indexed
- Cached
- Changed
- Analyzing
- Error

Example:

```
SYSTEM OVERVIEW

3 Services

✓ order-service
  commit a91fc20
  Cached

✓ inventory-service
  commit 12ab19f
  Cached

⚠ payment-service
  commit 9ff182a
  Changed
```

---

## 6. P0 — COMMIT-AWARE SEMANTIC CACHE

This is one of the primary features.

Every analyzed service must have a structured context associated with its Git state.

Recommended cache identity:

```
repository + branch + commitHash
```

Example:

```json
{
  "service": "order-service",
  "branch": "main",
  "commit": "a91fc20",
  "summary": "...",
  "apis": [],
  "database": [],
  "dependencies": [],
  "events": []
}
```

Required behavior:

- [ ] Read repository HEAD
- [ ] Compare HEAD with cached commit
- [ ] Cache hit → reuse existing context
- [ ] Cache miss → analyze repository
- [ ] Store generated context
- [ ] Display cache status in VSIX
- [ ] Store previous analyzed commit for incremental comparison

Example UI:

```
ORDER SERVICE

Commit:
a91fc20

Context:
✓ Cached

Files:
42

Last Analysis:
10:41:22

Estimated Context Reuse:
~31K tokens avoided
```

Any token-saving metric must be clearly presented as an estimate.

---

## 7. P0 — INCREMENTAL ANALYSIS

Do not automatically rescan an entire repository whenever HEAD changes.

Compare:

```
OLD COMMIT
a91fc20

NEW COMMIT
c821ad3
```

Use Git diff to identify changes.

Conceptually:

```
git diff --name-only a91fc20 c821ad3
```

Pipeline:

```
Commit changed
→ Git diff
→ Changed files
→ Classify files
→ Determine affected artifacts
→ Re-analyze affected context
→ Update Context Graph
→ Update cache
```

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect commit change
- [ ] Calculate Git diff
- [ ] Identify changed files
- [ ] Classify changed files
- [ ] Determine whether API is affected
- [ ] Determine whether database schema is affected
- [ ] Determine whether service dependency is affected
- [ ] Re-analyze changed service only
- [ ] Preserve unaffected service contexts
- [ ] Update cache
- [ ] Update Context Graph

---

## 8. P0 — API INTELLIGENCE

Extract REST APIs from each supported Spring Boot service.

Example:

```
Order Service

GET    /orders/{id}
POST   /orders
PUT    /orders/{id}
DELETE /orders/{id}
```

For each endpoint, attempt to capture:

- HTTP method
- Endpoint path
- Controller
- Request model
- Response model
- Related service dependencies
- Related database entities
- Semantic description

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect REST controllers
- [ ] Detect HTTP methods
- [ ] Detect endpoint paths
- [ ] Detect request models where possible
- [ ] Detect response models where possible
- [ ] Associate API with service
- [ ] Associate API with relevant entity where possible
- [ ] Generate short semantic description using watsonx

Example semantic description:

> "Creates an order, validates inventory availability, persists the order, and initiates payment."

---

## 9. P0 — DATABASE SCHEMA INTELLIGENCE

Extract basic database structure from Spring/JPA entities.

Example:

```
orders

├── id : UUID
├── customer_id : INTEGER
├── product_id : UUID
├── quantity : INTEGER
└── status : VARCHAR
```

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect JPA entities
- [ ] Detect table names
- [ ] Detect columns
- [ ] Detect basic data types
- [ ] Detect primary keys where possible
- [ ] Detect entity relationships
- [ ] Associate tables with services
- [ ] Store database schema in ServiceContext
- [ ] Add database nodes to Context Graph

Advanced Flyway/Liquibase support is P1, not required for P0.

---

## 10. P0 — SERVICE CONTEXT MODEL

Each service should produce a normalized ServiceContext.

Conceptual structure:

```
ServiceContext

├── identity
│   ├── serviceId
│   ├── repository
│   ├── branch
│   └── commitHash
│
├── APIs
│   ├── endpoints
│   ├── requestSchemas
│   └── responseSchemas
│
├── Database
│   ├── tables
│   ├── columns
│   └── relationships
│
├── Dependencies
│   ├── upstream
│   └── downstream
│
├── Events
│   ├── publishes
│   └── consumes
│
└── semanticSummary
```

Events can remain minimal or empty for the P0 demo if necessary.

---

## 11. P0 — SYSTEM CONTEXT GRAPH

Combine all ServiceContexts into a System Context Graph.

Example:

```
                  ORDER
                 SERVICE
                 /     \
                /       \
               v         v
        INVENTORY      PAYMENT
         SERVICE       SERVICE
            |             |
            v             v
       inventory_db   payment_db

              |
              v
           orders_db
```

Required node types:

- Service
- Database

Optional P1 node types:

- API
- Event
- Table

Required edges:

- Service → Service dependency
- Service → Database ownership/use

Checklist:

- [ ] Build graph from ServiceContexts
- [ ] Create service nodes
- [ ] Create database nodes
- [ ] Create dependency edges
- [ ] Create database edges
- [ ] Render graph in VSIX
- [ ] Support zoom
- [ ] Support pan
- [ ] Make nodes clickable
- [ ] Display selected node information
- [ ] Visually distinguish services and databases

The graph can be read-only. Do NOT build a graph editor.

---

## 12. P0 — CHANGE IMPACT ANALYSIS

This is the primary AI feature.

Example change:

```
orders.customer_id

INTEGER
→
UUID
```

Pipeline:

```
Git Diff
→ Change Detector
→ Context Graph
→ Retrieve Related Nodes
→ Structured Change Context
→ watsonx Runtime
→ Impact Reasoning
→ Bob + VSIX
```

Expected output:

```
CHANGE IMPACT

Change:
orders.customer_id
INTEGER → UUID

HIGH
payment-service

Reason:
OrderCreatedEvent currently expects an INTEGER customerId.

MEDIUM
Order REST API

Reason:
The customer identifier is exposed through the API contract.

LOW
Frontend

Reason:
The frontend already represents customer identifiers as strings.
```

Checklist:

- [ ] Detect API changes
- [ ] Detect database schema changes
- [ ] Identify affected graph nodes
- [ ] Retrieve related service contexts
- [ ] Construct scoped watsonx prompt/context
- [ ] Generate impact explanation
- [ ] Generate severity
- [ ] Explain WHY a component is affected
- [ ] Suggest affected components/files where possible
- [ ] Generate migration recommendations

Severity levels: **HIGH**, **MEDIUM**, **LOW**

Severity must include an explanation rather than only a label.

---

## 13. P0 — IBM WATSONX RUNTIME

watsonx must NOT be responsible for basic deterministic repository discovery when conventional tooling can do it more reliably.

Do NOT use:

```
Entire Repository → LLM → "Figure everything out"
```

Prefer:

```
Git + Parser + Structured Extraction
→ Structured Facts
→ Context Graph
→ Scoped Context
→ watsonx
→ Semantic Reasoning
```

watsonx responsibilities:

- [ ] Service semantic summaries
- [ ] API semantic descriptions
- [ ] Change interpretation
- [ ] Impact reasoning
- [ ] Severity reasoning
- [ ] Human-readable explanations
- [ ] Migration/change recommendations

The project should demonstrate that watsonx receives relevant scoped context instead of unnecessarily receiving the entire repository.

---

## 14. P0 — MCP SERVER

MCP is the primary integration contract between Bob and Bob Context Graph.

Minimum required MCP tools:

### `get_system_context()`

Returns:

- Services
- Current commit hashes
- Service relationships
- Database relationships
- System summary

### `get_service_context(service)`

Returns:

- Service identity
- Commit
- APIs
- Database schema
- Dependencies
- Semantic summary

### `analyze_change(service)`

Performs:

- Git diff
- Change classification
- Dependency lookup
- watsonx impact reasoning

Returns:

- Detected changes
- Affected components
- Severity
- Reasoning
- Recommended actions

### `refresh_context(service?)`

Allows Bob to explicitly refresh system intelligence.

- Refresh one service
- Optionally refresh all services
- Update cache
- Update graph

Optional MCP tools:

- `get_dependency_graph()`
- `get_database_schema()`
- `get_api_contract()`

Do not prioritize optional MCP tools until the four primary tools work.

---

## 15. P0 — IBM BOB MCP CONFIGURATION

The repository should include project-level Bob configuration.

Target:

```
.bob/
└── mcp.json
```

Configure Bob Context Graph MCP server so a developer cloning the repository can configure/run the integration with minimal manual work.

Checklist:

- [ ] Include `.bob/mcp.json`
- [ ] Document required environment variables
- [ ] Document watsonx credentials configuration
- [ ] Document MCP startup procedure
- [ ] Verify Bob discovers the MCP tools

Never commit credentials to Git.

---

## 16. P0 — BOB SKILL

Create:

```
.bob/
└── skills/
    └── context-graph/
        └── SKILL.md
```

The Skill should teach Bob that when a developer asks about:

- Architecture
- Microservice relationships
- API dependencies
- Database schema dependencies
- Breaking changes
- Change impact
- Blast radius
- Migration planning

Bob should query Bob Context Graph before independently rediscovering the entire repository.

Desired behavior:

> "When architectural or change-impact context is required, first query Bob Context Graph MCP. Prefer cached system context. Use `get_system_context()` for architecture questions. Use `get_service_context(service)` for service-specific questions. Use `analyze_change(service)` when evaluating a Git/API/database change. Inspect raw source code only when implementation-level details unavailable from the context graph are required."

Checklist:

- [ ] Create Skill
- [ ] Describe appropriate triggers
- [ ] Describe available MCP tools
- [ ] Tell Bob to prefer cached context
- [ ] Test at least one architecture question
- [ ] Test at least one impact-analysis question

---

## 17. P0 — VS CODE EXTENSION / VSIX

The VS Code extension is the visual interface for developers. It is NOT the primary Bob integration layer.

Responsibilities:

- Display system state
- Display services
- Display cache state
- Display dependency graph
- Display detected changes
- Display impact analysis

Minimum sidebar:

```
BOB CONTEXT GRAPH

SYSTEM

● 3 services
● 7 APIs
● 3 databases

✓ inventory-service
✓ payment-service

IMPACT ANALYSIS

⚠ 2 HIGH
⚠ 1 MEDIUM
✓ 1 LOW

[ Open System Graph ]

---

## 18. P0 — GRAPH WEBVIEW

Example:

│ Bob Context Graph              HEAD: c821ad3     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

## 19. P0 — IMPACT VISUALIZATION

## 25. GOLDEN-PATH DEMO

The entire implementation should prioritize this demo scenario.

### SCENE 1 — PROBLEM

### SCENE 2 — INITIAL SYSTEM UNDERSTANDING

### SCENE 4 — INTRODUCE BREAKING CHANGE

### SCENE 5 — INCREMENTAL INTELLIGENCE

```

### SCENE 6 — IMPACT ANALYSIS

Click "Analyze Impact". Visual graph highlights payment-service as HIGH. Impact report generated by watsonx.

### SCENE 7 — BOB COMPLETES THE LOOP

## 27. PRODUCT POSITIONING

Primary description:

> "Bob Context Graph extends IBM Bob with persistent, commit-aware system intelligence, allowing Bob to understand microservice APIs, database schemas, dependencies, and the blast radius of changes without repeatedly rediscovering the entire codebase."

Short pitch:

> "Bob shouldn't rediscover your system every time you ask a question."

Alternative pitch:

> "Your code tells Bob what exists. Bob Context Graph tells Bob what depends on it and what could break."

Core architecture message:

- **VSIX = See it.**
- **MCP = Access it.**
- **Skill = Know when to use it.**
- **watsonx = Reason about it.**
- **Bob = Act on it.**

---

## 28. IMPLEMENTATION PRINCIPLE

Prioritize, in this order:

1. Working end-to-end integration
2. Change-impact analysis
3. Commit-aware caching
4. Dependency visualization
5. Bob integration
6. Visual polish
7. Additional features

Whenever there is a choice between building another feature and improving the golden-path demo, improve the golden-path demo.

The hackathon prototype does not need to solve every microservice architecture problem. It needs to convincingly demonstrate one idea:

**IBM Bob can maintain persistent knowledge of a microservice system, incrementally update that knowledge when the code changes, and use watsonx to reason about the impact of those changes before the developer acts.**
